paper.title: DSSSB TGT Mathematics 2021 (13 September, female)
paper.source: DSSSB TGT Mathematics (Female), computer-based test of 13 September 2021, 12:30 to 2:30 pm: the mathematics section (questions 101 to 190) of the board's response sheet as re-shared after the exam, with the board's answer key
paper.note: The mathematics section of the paper; the whole paper had 200 questions in 120 minutes.

en.q: What condition holds for perpendicularity of 2 vectors?
options: one of the two vectors is zero
en.explanation: For non-zero vectors, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta$. This is $0$ exactly when $\theta=90^\circ$, so perpendicular vectors have zero dot product.
notes: Equal vectors are parallel, not perpendicular.
A zero vector makes the dot product $0$ trivially; that is not the test.
A zero cross product means the vectors are parallel.
facts: $\vec a\perp\vec b\iff\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$; $\vec a\parallel\vec b\iff\vec a\times\vec b=\vec 0$.

en.q: The graph of a quadratic equation $y=ax^2+bx+c$ is a parabola, when it will be upwards and downwards curve?
options: it will be open upwards if $a>0$ and downwards if $a<0$
it will be open upwards if $a<0$ and downwards if $a>0$
it will never be open upwards
it will never be open downwards
en.explanation: $y''=2a$. If $a>0$ the parabola is concave up: it opens upwards with a minimum at the vertex $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$. If $a<0$ it opens downwards with a maximum there.
notes: Correct: the sign of $a$ decides the opening.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $y=ax^2+bx+c$ opens upwards if $a>0$, downwards if $a<0$; vertex at $x=-b/(2a)$.

en.q: When the fluid $(F)$ is incompressible then which of following condition holds?
en.explanation: For an incompressible fluid no volume element gains or loses fluid, so the net outflow per unit volume is zero: the velocity field is solenoidal, $\nabla\cdot\vec F=0$.
notes: The fluid need not be at rest.
Non-zero divergence means sources or sinks (compression or expansion).
No scalar product is involved in the condition.
facts: Incompressible flow: $\nabla\cdot\vec F=0$ (solenoidal); irrotational flow: $\nabla\times\vec F=\vec 0$.

en.q: If $f$ be a function defined in $[a,b]$ and is twice differentiable, then it is said to be concave upwards if:
en.explanation: Concave upwards (convex) means the slope $f'$ keeps increasing, i.e. $f''(x)>0$ on $[a,b]$; the curve lies above its tangents. Example: $f(x)=x^2$, $f''=2>0$.
facts: $f''>0$: concave up (holds water); $f''<0$: concave down; a sign change of $f''$ marks a point of inflexion.

en.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius $a$ is
en.explanation: Surface area of a sphere $=4\pi r^2=4\pi a^2$ (its volume is $\frac43\pi a^3$).
notes: An area of a sphere cannot be $0$.
facts: Sphere: $S=4\pi r^2$, $V=\frac43\pi r^3$; hemisphere (total) $3\pi r^2$.

en.q: The inverse of $3$ modulo $7$ is ______?
en.explanation: $3\cdot5=15=2\cdot7+1\equiv1\pmod 7$, so $3^{-1}\equiv5\equiv-2\pmod 7$. Check: $3(-2)=-6\equiv1\pmod 7$.
facts: The inverse of $a$ mod $m$ exists iff $\gcd(a,m)=1$; find it by trial or by the Euclidean algorithm.

en.q: If $\vec A=2\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec B=4\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$, find $\vec A\cdot\vec B$?
notes: $10=8+1+1$: the sign of the $\hat k$ term was ignored.
facts: $\vec A\cdot\vec B=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3$.

en.q: The points $a,b,c,d$, taken in that order, in the complex plane are the vertices of a parallelogram if ___?
en.explanation: In a parallelogram $abcd$ the diagonals $ac$ and $bd$ bisect each other, so their midpoints coincide: $\frac{a+c}2=\frac{b+d}2$, i.e. $a+c=b+d$ (equivalently $b-a=c-d$).
notes: This pairs adjacent vertices; it is not the diagonal condition.
This says $b$ is the midpoint of $ac$: the points are collinear.
Correct: the diagonals have a common midpoint.
facts: $a,b,c,d$ (in order) form a parallelogram iff $a+c=b+d$.

en.q: Which of the following is correct for the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x-1$?
options: it has local maximum at $3$ but has no local minimum
it has local maximum at $-1$ and local minimum at $3$
it has local maximum at $3$ and local minimum at $-2$
it neither has local maximum nor local minimum
notes: $x=3$ is the minimum, not the maximum.
$x=-2$ is not even a stationary point.
A cubic with two distinct stationary points has both extrema.
facts: For a cubic with $a>0$, the smaller stationary point is the maximum and the larger is the minimum.

en.q: Which theorem states that "Every bounded sequence has at least a limit point"?
en.explanation: Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem: every bounded sequence of real numbers has at least one limit point, i.e. a convergent subsequence (and every bounded infinite set has a limit point).
notes: The Riesz representation theorem is about linear functionals.
The sandwich theorem gives a limit squeezed between two others.
An initial value problem is a differential equation with a starting condition.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Bolzano–Weierstrass: every bounded sequence in $\mathbb R$ has a convergent subsequence.

en.q: If $|A|=4$, find the number of partitions of $A$?
en.explanation: The number of partitions of an $n$-element set is the Bell number $B_n$. For $n=4$ count by block sizes: $4$: $1$; $3+1$: $4$; $2+2$: $3$; $2+1+1$: $6$; $1+1+1+1$: $1$. Total $1+4+3+6+1=15$.
facts: Bell numbers $B_0,\dots,B_5=1,1,2,5,15,52$; $B_n$ also counts the equivalence relations on an $n$-set.

en.q: To reduce the matrix to row echelon form the leading entry of each row must be?
en.explanation: In row echelon form (as usually defined in Indian textbooks) the first non-zero entry of each non-zero row is $1$ (a leading $1$), each leading $1$ lies to the right of the one above, and zero rows come last. (Books that only require a non-zero leading entry in echelon form still normalise it to $1$ in the reduced form; $1$ is the only option that is a rule.)
notes: The leading entry is by definition the first non-zero entry.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: Echelon form: leading $1$s step to the right going down, zero rows at the bottom; rank = number of non-zero rows.

en.q: When is a curve said to be symmetric about the pole or origin?
options: if curve changes when $r$ is replaced by $2r$
if curve changes when $r$ is replaced by $-r$
if curve doesn't change when $r$ is replaced by $-r$
if curve doesn't change when $r$ is replaced by $2r$
en.explanation: $(r,\theta)$ and $(-r,\theta)$ are reflections of each other in the pole. So a polar curve is symmetric about the pole when its equation is unchanged on replacing $r$ by $-r$ (e.g. $r^2=a^2\cos2\theta$).
notes: If the equation changes, the test for symmetry fails.
Replacing $r$ by $2r$ tests nothing about symmetry.
facts: Polar symmetry: $\theta\to-\theta$ unchanged: about the initial line; $r\to-r$ unchanged: about the pole.

en.q: Which of the following is not included in general method to draw an algebraic curve for tracing?
en.explanation: Curve tracing checks symmetry, the origin and intercepts, tangents (at the origin and parallel to the axes), asymptotes, the region where the curve exists, and special points. Orthogonality is not one of the steps.
notes: Tangents at the origin are a standard step.
The region of existence is a standard step.
facts: Curve tracing: symmetry, origin, intercepts, tangents, asymptotes, region, special points.

en.q: Find the number of anti symmetric relations on set $A$ having $2$ elements?
en.explanation: Each diagonal pair $(a,a)$ may be in or out: $2^n$ ways. For each pair $a\ne b$, of $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$ we may take neither or exactly one: $3$ ways. So the count is $2^n\cdot3^{n(n-1)/2}=2^2\cdot3^1=12$.
notes: $16=2^4$ is the number of all relations on a 2-element set.
facts: On an $n$-set: relations $2^{n^2}$; reflexive $2^{n^2-n}$; symmetric $2^{n(n+1)/2}$; antisymmetric $2^n3^{n(n-1)/2}$.

en.q: Let $A$ be an $n\times m$ matrix with each entry equal to $+1$, $-1$ or $0$ such that every column has exactly one $+1$ and exactly one $-1$. Then what can you say about rank of the matrix?
en.explanation: Every column sums to $(+1)+(-1)=0$, so adding all $n$ rows gives the zero row. The rows are linearly dependent, hence $\operatorname{rank}A\le n-1$. (Equality holds only when the corresponding graph is connected.)
notes: Columns can repeat, e.g. two equal columns.
Not always: two disjoint blocks give rank $n-2$.
The rows are always dependent, so rank $<n$.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: If the rows of a matrix add up to zero, its rank is at most (number of rows) $-1$.

en.q: Euler function is:
en.explanation: $\phi(1)=\phi(2)=1$, so $\phi$ is not one-one. $\phi(n)$ is even for every $n\ge3$, so odd values such as $3$ are never taken: $\phi$ is not onto $\mathbb N$.
facts: $\phi(n)$ is even for $n\ge3$; $\phi(p)=p-1$ for a prime $p$.

en.q: Identify the set in which supremum of set is equal to infimum of the set?
en.explanation: For a non-empty bounded set, $\inf S\le x\le\sup S$ for every $x\in S$. So $\sup S=\inf S$ forces every element to equal that number: $S$ is a singleton $\{a\}$.
notes: For $\emptyset$ every real is a bound: $\sup\emptyset=-\infty<\inf\emptyset=+\infty$.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: $\sup S=\inf S$ iff $S$ is a singleton.

en.q: The congruence relation $ax\equiv b\pmod m$ has a unique solution if?
en.explanation: Let $d=\gcd(a,m)$. Then $ax\equiv b\pmod m$ is solvable iff $d\mid b$, and then it has exactly $d$ incongruent solutions mod $m$. A unique solution means $d=1$.
notes: $d=m$ means $a\equiv0$: no solution or all $m$ residues.
facts: $ax\equiv b\pmod m$: solvable iff $d=\gcd(a,m)\mid b$; then exactly $d$ solutions mod $m$.

en.q: Find the limit of function $f(x,y)=x+2y$ as $(x,y)\to(1,2)$?
en.explanation: $f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous, so the limit is its value: $1+2(2)=5$.
facts: For a continuous function, the limit at a point equals the value there.

en.q: For what value of $k$ does the function $f(x,y)=3xy$, where $(x,y)\ne(2,3)$, and $k$ whenever $(x,y)=(2,3)$, become continuous at $(2,3)$?
en.explanation: Continuity at $(2,3)$ needs $k=\lim_{(x,y)\to(2,3)}3xy=3\cdot2\cdot3=18$. (The paper omits the words 'become continuous at $(2,3)$'; continuity is the only property for which $k$ matters.)
facts: To remove a point discontinuity, define the value as the limit there.

en.q: Logistic growth equation is given by?
en.explanation: The logistic model is $\frac{dN}{dt}=rN\left(1-\frac NK\right)=rN\frac{K-N}{K}$, where $r$ is the intrinsic growth rate and $K$ the carrying capacity. Growth is nearly exponential for small $N$ and stops at $N=K$.
notes: Not divided by $K$, so $r$ loses its meaning as the per-capita rate.
Dividing by $K-N$ would make growth blow up near $K$.
facts: Logistic: $\frac{dN}{dt}=rN(1-\frac NK)$, an S-shaped curve levelling off at $K$; exponential: $\frac{dN}{dt}=rN$.

en.q: Local minimizer $u$ of $J$ is isolated if there exists $p>0$ and for $u$ in $S$ we have?
en.explanation: A local minimizer $u$ is strict (isolated) if there is $p>0$ such that $J(u)<J(v)$ for every $v\in S$ with $0<\|v-u\|<p$: no other nearby point gives a value as small. (The paper prints 'for $u$ in $S$'; it means every $v\ne u$ in $S$ with $\|v-u\|<p$. 'Isolated' is used here in the sense of a strict local minimizer.)
notes: Correct: a strict inequality for all nearby $v\ne u$.
This would make $u$ a local maximizer.
facts: Local minimum: $J(u)\le J(v)$ near $u$; strict (isolated) local minimum: $J(u)<J(v)$ for $v\ne u$ near $u$.

en.q: The infinite series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\cos(1/n)$ is?
en.explanation: $\cos\frac1n\to\cos0=1\ne0$, so the $n$th-term test fails: the series cannot converge. Its terms are positive, so it diverges to $+\infty$.
notes: A series of positive terms cannot oscillate.
facts: If $\sum a_n$ converges then $a_n\to0$; terms not tending to $0$ means divergence.

en.q: Find the limit point of the sequence $\langle 1+1/n\rangle$?
en.explanation: $1+\frac1n\to1$, so every neighbourhood of $1$ contains infinitely many terms, and no other point does. The only limit point is $1$.
notes: $2$ is the first term, taken only once.
$0$ is the limit of $\frac1n$, not of $1+\frac1n$.
facts: A convergent sequence has exactly one limit point, its limit.

en.q: Find the limit of the function $f(n)=1/n$ where $n$ approaches infinity
en.explanation: For $n>\frac1\epsilon$, $0<\frac1n<\epsilon$; hence $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n=0$.
notes: $1$ is the value at $n=1$, not the limit.
facts: $\frac1{n^p}\to0$ for every $p>0$.

en.q: Let $A=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|>1\}$, $B=\{z\in\mathbb C:z\ne0\}$. Then which is the false statement?
options: there is a continuous onto function $f:A\to B$
there is a non constant analytic function $f:A\to B$
there is a non constant analytic function $f:B\to A$
there is a continuous one to one function $f:B\to A$
en.explanation: Suppose $f:B\to A$ is analytic. Then $g=\frac1f$ is analytic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ with $|g|<1$. A bounded isolated singularity is removable, so $g$ is a bounded entire function, constant by Liouville's theorem. Hence (c) is false. The others hold: $f(z)=(|z|-1)\frac{z}{|z|}$ for (a), $f(z)=z$ for (b), $f(z)=z+\frac{z}{|z|}$ for (d).
notes: False, by Riemann's removable singularity theorem and Liouville.
True: $z+\frac z{|z|}$ is one-one with modulus $|z|+1>1$.
facts: A function analytic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and bounded is constant (removable singularity + Liouville).

en.q: Which rule is used to calculate limits when the function reaches to indeterminate forms?
en.explanation: For the forms $\frac00$ and $\frac\infty\infty$: $\lim\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\lim\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$ (L'Hospital's rule). Other forms ($0\cdot\infty$, $\infty-\infty$, $1^\infty$, ...) are first rewritten into these. E.g. $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\cos x}{1}=1$.
notes: Leibnitz's rule gives the $n$th derivative of a product.
facts: L'Hospital: for $\frac00$ or $\frac\infty\infty$, differentiate numerator and denominator separately.

en.q: If $L$ be a limit point of the sequence $\langle A\rangle$ then there exists a subsequence $\langle B\rangle$ of the sequence $\langle A\rangle$ which converges to?
en.explanation: $L$ is a limit point of $\langle a_n\rangle$ when every neighbourhood of $L$ contains $a_n$ for infinitely many $n$. Choose $n_1<n_2<\dots$ with $|a_{n_k}-L|<\frac1k$; this subsequence converges to $L$.
facts: Limit points of a sequence = limits of its convergent subsequences.

en.q: The solution of the initial value problem $xy'-y=0$ with $y(1)=1$ is?
en.explanation: Separate: $\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{dx}{x}$, so $\ln|y|=\ln|x|+c$ and $y=Cx$. $y(1)=1$ gives $C=1$: $y=x$.
facts: $xy'=y$ has the solutions $y=Cx$ (lines through the origin).

en.q: Change in number of individuals in population over a period of time is called ____
en.explanation: The change in the number of individuals of a population over time is called population growth. Exponential (J-shaped) and logistic or sigmoid (S-shaped) growth are particular models of it.
facts: Exponential growth: $\frac{dN}{dt}=rN$; logistic growth: $\frac{dN}{dt}=rN(1-\frac NK)$.

en.q: What will we do to make the given differential equation exact?
options: we divide it by its derivatives
we do integration on both sides
we multiply it with integrating factor
en.explanation: If $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ is not exact ($M_y\ne N_x$), multiply it by an integrating factor $\mu$ chosen so that $(\mu M)_y=(\mu N)_x$. E.g. if $\frac{M_y-N_x}{N}=f(x)$, then $\mu=e^{\int f(x)\,dx}$.
notes: Integration comes after the equation is exact.
facts: $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ is exact iff $\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}$; otherwise look for an integrating factor.

en.q: The infinite series $-1-3-5-7-\dots$ diverges to?
en.explanation: The partial sums are $S_n=-(1+3+\dots+(2n-1))=-n^2\to-\infty$, so the series diverges to $-\infty$.

en.q: Pick the true statement
options: series always converges to a finite number
Every convergent sequence is Cauchy sequence
every convergent sequence is not bounded
en.explanation: If $a_n\to L$, then for $m,n\ge N$: $|a_m-a_n|\le|a_m-L|+|L-a_n|<\frac\epsilon2+\frac\epsilon2=\epsilon$. So every convergent sequence is Cauchy (in $\mathbb R$ the converse also holds).
notes: In $\mathbb R$ every Cauchy sequence converges.
facts: In $\mathbb R$: convergent $\iff$ Cauchy (completeness); convergent $\Rightarrow$ bounded.

en.q: Function $f(x,y)$ is said to be continuous at $(a,b)$ whenever $|f(x,y)-f(a,b)|<\epsilon$ if?
en.explanation: $f$ is continuous at $(a,b)$ if for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x,y)-f(a,b)|<\epsilon$ whenever $|x-a|<\delta$ and $|y-b|<\delta$ together. One condition alone does not bring $(x,y)$ close to $(a,b)$. (Option (b) is cut off in the paper; 'both' refers to the two conditions $|x-a|<\delta$ and $|y-b|<\delta$ of options (c) and (d).)
notes: Correct: both coordinates must be close.
facts: Continuity at $(a,b)$: $\forall\epsilon\,\exists\delta$: $|x-a|<\delta$, $|y-b|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x,y)-f(a,b)|<\epsilon$.

en.q: Let $A$ is a subset of $\mathbb R$ and $f:A\to\mathbb R$ is given by $f(x)=x^2$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous if?
en.explanation: If $|x|\le M$ on $A$, then $|x^2-y^2|=|x+y||x-y|\le2M|x-y|$, so $f$ is Lipschitz and hence uniformly continuous. On $\mathbb R$ it is not: $(n+\frac1n)^2-n^2>2$ although the points are only $\frac1n$ apart.
notes: $\mathbb R$ is dense and $x^2$ is not uniformly continuous on it.
facts: $x^2$ is uniformly continuous on every bounded set, but not on $\mathbb R$.

en.q: The area bounded by the curve $y=2\sqrt x$, $y=-x$, $x=1$ and $x=4$ is given by?
en.explanation: On $[1,4]$, $2\sqrt x>-x$. Area $=\int_1^4(2\sqrt x+x)\,dx=\left[\frac43x^{3/2}+\frac{x^2}2\right]_1^4$, which is $\frac{28}3+\frac{15}2=\frac{101}6$.
facts: Area between curves $=\int_a^b(y_{\text{upper}}-y_{\text{lower}})\,dx$.

en.q: Function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, $P$ and $Q$ are partitions of $[a,b]$ s.t. $P$ is contained in $Q$, then?
options: one is true other is false
en.explanation: $Q\supseteq P$ is a refinement of $P$. Splitting a subinterval can only raise the infimum on each piece, so lower sums increase, $L(f,P)\le L(f,Q)$; likewise upper sums decrease, $U(f,Q)\le U(f,P)$.
notes: Always $L(f,P)\le U(f,Q)$, the other way round.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: Refining a partition raises lower sums and lowers upper sums; every lower sum $\le$ every upper sum.

en.q: Find radius of convergence of $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(x-7)^{n+1}}{n^n}$?
en.explanation: Here the coefficients are $\frac1{n^n}$; shifting the power by one does not change the radius. $\left|\frac1{n^n}\right|^{1/n}=\frac1n\to0$, so $\frac1R=0$ and $R=\infty$: the series converges for every $x$. (The paper prints the exponent as $((n+1)/n^n)$, a bracket slip for $(x-7)^{n+1}/n^n$.)
facts: Cauchy–Hadamard: $\frac1R=\limsup|a_n|^{1/n}$; $\frac1{n^n}$ and $\frac1{n!}$ give $R=\infty$.

en.q: For the function to be Riemann integrable what will be the condition in terms of affecting the power series?
options: lower integral is less than upper integral
lower integral is same as upper integral
en.explanation: For a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$, the lower integral $\sup_PL(f,P)$ and the upper integral $\inf_PU(f,P)$ always exist, and lower $\le$ upper. $f$ is Riemann integrable exactly when they are equal; the common value is $\int_a^bf$. (The words 'in terms of affecting the power series' in the stem have no meaning here and are ignored.)
notes: Strict inequality means not integrable (e.g. Dirichlet's function).
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: $f\in R[a,b]\iff$ lower integral $=$ upper integral $\iff$ for each $\epsilon$ some $P$ has $U-L<\epsilon$.

en.q: Pick the wrong statement?
options: discontinuity always occurs at upper limit
Discontinuity occurs at both upper and lower limits of the function
Improper integral of 2nd kind has discontinuity at lower limit
Improper integral of 2nd kind has discontinuity at upper limit
en.explanation: In an improper integral of the second kind the integrand is unbounded at the lower limit (e.g. $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt x}$), at the upper limit (e.g. $\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x}}$), at both ends, or inside the interval. So 'always at the upper limit' is wrong. Options (b)–(d) describe cases that can occur; only (a) claims something always happens, and that is false.
notes: Wrong: it can be at the lower limit, both ends or inside.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: First kind: infinite limit of integration; second kind: integrand unbounded at some point of a finite interval.

en.q: The divergence of a vector field $\vec A$ is always equal to zero if the vector field $\vec A$ can be expressed as?
options: the curl of any vector field
en.explanation:
If $\vec A=
abla	imes\vec B$, then $
abla\cdot\vec A=
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\vec B)=0$ identically, because the mixed partial derivatives cancel in pairs. A gradient gives $
abla\cdot
abla\phi=
abla^2\phi$, which is not always $0$.
notes: The divergence of a vector field is a scalar, not a vector field.
Divergence is not defined for a scalar field.
facts:
$

en.q: If $\vec R$ is the position vector, then $\operatorname{div}\vec R$ is equal to
en.explanation: $\vec R=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$, so $\nabla\cdot\vec R=\frac{\partial x}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial y}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial z}=3$.
notes: That is the value in the plane ($x\hat i+y\hat j$).
facts:
For $\vec r=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$: $
abla\cdot\vec r=3$, $
abla	imes\vec r=\vec 0$, $
abla r= rac{\vec r}{r}$.

en.q: Which of the following function contains odd terms in the expansion of Taylor's series?
en.explanation: $\sin(x^3)=x^3-\frac{x^9}{3!}+\frac{x^{15}}{5!}-\dots$ has only odd powers; it is an odd function. $\cos(x^2)$, $\sin(x^2)$ and $\cos(x^3)$ are even functions, so their Maclaurin series contain only even powers.
facts: An odd function has only odd powers in its Maclaurin series; an even function only even powers.

en.q: Green's theorem is used to?
en.explanation: Green's theorem $\oint_C(M\,dx+N\,dy)=\iint_R(N_x-M_y)\,dA$ turns line integrals round a plane curve into double integrals. It gives the circulation and flux of plane (2-D) flows, and areas $\frac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$. The textbook use, area of a plane region, is not offered: plane figures have no volume (a), Green's theorem does not give perimeters (d), and (c) is meaningless, so (b) is the answer.
notes: Plane figures have area, not volume.
The key: plane-flow circulation and flux.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: Green: $\oint_C(M\,dx+N\,dy)=\iint_R(N_x-M_y)\,dA$; area $=\frac12\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$.

en.q: The necessary and sufficient condition for Taylor's theorem is that?
en.explanation: Taylor's theorem of order $n$ needs $f^{(n-1)}$ continuous on $[a,a+h]$ and $f^{(n)}$ to exist in $(a,a+h)$; that is, $f$ must have the higher derivatives. Continuity alone is not enough. ('Necessary and sufficient' is loose wording: the existence of the higher derivatives is the hypothesis of the theorem.)
notes: Then no Taylor expansion is possible.
facts: Taylor: $f(a+h)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{h^k}{k!}f^{(k)}(a)+R_n$ with $R_n=\frac{h^n}{n!}f^{(n)}(a+\theta h)$, $0<\theta<1$.

en.q: The line integrals can be converted to surface integral using ------- in multiply connected domain?
en.explanation: Green's theorem converts a line integral round the boundary of a plane region into a double (surface) integral over the region. For a multiply connected region the boundary includes the inner curves, traversed so that the region stays on the left.
notes: The Cauchy–Riemann equations are about analyticity.
No such theorem; Baire's theorem is about category.
The sandwich theorem is about limits.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: Green (plane), Stokes (surface) and Gauss (volume) theorems all change the dimension of an integral by one.

en.q: Find the value of $f(x,y)=8x+5y-7$ at $(x,y)=(1,2)$
facts: Evaluate a function of two variables by substituting both coordinates.

en.q: A function is said to be Riemann integrable over $[a,b]$ s.t. any number $L$ lying between $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P)$ s.t. for $\epsilon>0$ s.t.?
en.explanation: $f$ is integrable with integral $L$ iff for every $\epsilon>0$ there is a partition $P$ with $L(f,P)\le L\le U(f,P)$ and both gaps small: $U(f,P)-L<\epsilon$ and $L-L(f,P)<\epsilon$. This is Riemann's criterion $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\epsilon$. (The stem is garbled in the paper; read: $f$ is integrable with integral $L$ if for each $\epsilon>0$ some partition $P$ satisfies the condition asked.)
notes: The gap must become small, not stay large.
The gap must become small, not stay large.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: Riemann's criterion: $f$ is integrable iff for every $\epsilon>0$ some partition has $U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\epsilon$.

en.q: Find the interior of $\{1,2,3,4\}$?
en.explanation: A point is interior if some interval $(p-\epsilon,p+\epsilon)$ lies inside the set. No interval fits inside a finite set of reals, so the interior is $\emptyset$.
notes: No interval around $3$ lies in the set.
No interval around $1$ lies in the set.
No interval around $2$ lies in the set.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: In $\mathbb R$ a finite set is closed and has empty interior.

en.q: If $p$ and $q$ are positive numbers and $p^2+q^2=1$ then maximum value of $p+q$ is?
en.explanation: $(p+q)^2=p^2+q^2+2pq\le2(p^2+q^2)=2$, so $p+q\le\sqrt2$, with equality at $p=q=\frac1{\sqrt2}$. (Or $p=\cos\theta$, $q=\sin\theta$: $p+q=\sqrt2\sin(\theta+45^\circ)$.)
facts: If $p^2+q^2=1$ then $p+q\le\sqrt2$ (QM–AM inequality).

en.q: Evaluate the double integral $\iint_Rx\sin(x+y)\,dx\,dy$ over $R=[0,\pi]\times[0,\frac\pi2]$?
en.explanation:
Inner: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(x+y)\,dy=\cos x-\cos(x+\frac\pi2)=\cos x+\sin x$.
Outer: $\int_0^\pi x\cos x\,dx=[x\sin x+\cos x]_0^\pi=-2$ and $\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx=[\sin x-x\cos x]_0^\pi=\pi$.
Total $=\pi-2$.
notes: The sign of $\int_0^\pi x\cos x\,dx=-2$ was lost.
facts: $\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx=\pi$ and $\int_0^\pi x\cos x\,dx=-2$.

en.q: The limit points of $\langle1,0,2,1,0,2,1,0,2,\dots\rangle$ is/are:
en.explanation: Each of the values $1$, $0$, $2$ occurs infinitely often, giving constant subsequences, so each is a limit point. No other number is approached.
facts: A value taken infinitely many times by a sequence is a limit point of the sequence.

en.q: The set of limit points of a sequence is:
en.explanation: The set of subsequential limits of a real sequence is always closed: if limit points $L_k\to L$, pick terms within $\frac1k$ of $L_k$ with increasing indices; they converge to $L$, so $L$ is again a limit point.
notes: Only $\emptyset$ and $\mathbb R$ are both; it happens but not in general.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: The set of limit points (derived set) is always closed.

en.q: Which property does not hold as a binary operation in groups?
en.explanation: A group operation must be associative. Subtraction is not: $(5-3)-1=1$ but $5-(3-1)=3$. So, e.g., $(\mathbb Z,-)$ is not a group, while $(\mathbb Z,+)$, $(\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\},\times)$ and invertible matrices under multiplication are groups.
notes: Non-singular matrices form a group under multiplication.
Non-zero rationals form a group under multiplication.
facts: Subtraction and division are not associative, so they never give groups.

en.q: If $f(z)=u+iv$ is an analytic function in domain $D$ then?
en.explanation:
By the Cauchy–Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$: $
abla u\cdot
abla v=u_xv_x+u_yv_y=-u_xu_y+u_yu_x=0$. So the level curves $u=c_1$ and $v=c_2$ cut at right angles (where $f'
e0$).
notes: They meet at right angles, not parallel.
True but says nothing; they meet at right angles.
facts: For analytic $u+iv$, the families $u=c_1$ and $v=c_2$ are orthogonal trajectories.

en.q: A linear operator defined by $T$ in metric space is said to be bounded iff?
en.explanation: A linear operator $T$ on a normed space is bounded iff there is a constant $k$ with $\|T(x)\|\le k\|x\|$ for all $x$. For linear maps, bounded $\iff$ continuous. (In the option the strict $<$ should be $\le$, since $x=0$ gives $0<0$; and the space should be a normed space.)
notes: The norm of a vector always exists.
facts: $T$ linear is bounded iff $\|Tx\|\le k\|x\|$ for all $x$; then $\|T\|$ is the least such $k$.

en.q: A set $G$ with one binary operation which is closed as well as associative is called?
en.explanation: Closed only: groupoid. Closed and associative: semigroup. Adding an identity: monoid. Adding inverses as well: group.
facts: Groupoid $\subset$ semigroup (associative) $\subset$ monoid (identity) $\subset$ group (inverses).

en.q: A metric space $X$ is said to be complete if
options: every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges in $X$
every convergent sequence in it is bounded
every Cauchy sequence in $X$ has more than 2 convergent subsequences
Cauchy sequence in $X$ is not convergent
en.explanation: By definition $X$ is complete when every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges to a point of $X$. $\mathbb R$ is complete; $\mathbb Q$ is not ($1,1.4,1.41,\dots\to\sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q$).
notes: True in every metric space, so it defines nothing.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Complete: every Cauchy sequence converges in the space ($\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, closed subsets of them).

en.q: A metric space defined by $\{d(x,y)=r\text{ for all }x,y\in\mathbb R\}$ is called as
en.explanation: In a metric space, $S(x_0,r)=\{x:d(x,x_0)=r\}$, the points at distance exactly $r$ from a centre, is the sphere. $\{x:d(x,x_0)<r\}$ is the open ball and $\{x:d(x,x_0)\le r\}$ the closed ball. (The stem is garbled in the paper: it describes the set $\{x:d(x,y)=r\}$ for a fixed centre $y$, not a metric space.)
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Sphere: $d=r$; open ball: $d<r$; closed ball: $d\le r$.

en.q: Which is known as multiplicative identity of group with respect to external binary operation?
en.explanation: The multiplicative identity is $1$: $1\cdot x=x\cdot1=x$. For an external operation such as scalar multiplication, $1\cdot v=v$. $0$ is the additive identity.
facts: Additive identity $0$ ($a+0=a$); multiplicative identity $1$ ($a\cdot1=a$).

en.q: Find the domain of the function defined by $f(z)=\frac{z}{z+\bar z}$ where $\bar z$ denotes complex conjugate of $z$?
en.explanation: $z+\bar z=2\operatorname{Re}(z)$, so $f(z)=\frac{z}{2\operatorname{Re}(z)}$ is defined exactly when $\operatorname{Re}(z)\ne0$: the plane minus the imaginary axis.
notes: Real $z\ne0$ are allowed, but not only them.
These are exactly the points excluded.
facts: $z+\bar z=2\operatorname{Re}z$, $z-\bar z=2i\operatorname{Im}z$, $z\bar z=|z|^2$.

en.q: Let $A$ be a subset of $\mathbb R$. Which of the following properties imply $A$ is compact?
options: there is no one one and continuous function from $A$ onto $(0,1)$
Every continuous function $f$ from $A$ to $\mathbb R$ is bounded
there exists a continuous function from $A$ onto $[0,1]$
Every sequence $\{x_n\}$ in $A$ has no convergent subsequence converging to a point in $A$
en.explanation: If $A$ is unbounded, $f(x)=x$ is continuous and unbounded. If $A$ is not closed, with a limit point $p\notin A$, then $f(x)=\frac1{|x-p|}$ is continuous and unbounded. So (b) forces $A$ closed and bounded, i.e. compact (Heine–Borel).
notes: $[0,1)$ satisfies it (a continuous one-one image of $[0,1)$ is half-open) but is not compact.
$\mathbb R$ maps onto $[0,1]$ by $|\sin x|$ but is not compact.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ is compact iff closed and bounded iff every continuous real function on $A$ is bounded.

en.q: For any two subsets $X$ and $Y$ let $X+Y=\{x+y:x\in X,y\in Y\}$ then find the wrong one?
options: if $X$ is closed, $Y$ is compact then $X+Y$ is closed
if $X$ and $Y$ are compact then $X+Y$ is compact
If $X$ and $Y$ are closed then $X+Y$ is closed
if $X$ and $Y$ are open sets then $X+Y$ is open
en.explanation: Counter-example in $\mathbb R$: $X=\{n:n\ge2\}$ and $Y=\{-n+\frac1n:n\ge2\}$ are closed (no finite limit points). $X+Y$ contains every $\frac1n$ but not $0$, so it is not closed. The other statements are true.
notes: True: use a convergent subsequence from compact $Y$.
True: continuous image of the compact set $X\times Y$.
True: $X+Y=\bigcup_{y\in Y}(X+y)$, a union of open sets.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Closed + compact is closed, compact + compact is compact, open + anything is open, but closed + closed need not be closed.

en.q: Continuous function $C[a,b]$ from $a$ to $b$ is called
en.explanation: A function continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ is bounded and attains its bounds (extreme value theorem). So every $f\in C[a,b]$ is a bounded function. (The stem is garbled in the paper; it is read as 'a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is'.)
notes: Only on open or unbounded intervals, e.g. $\frac1x$ on $(0,1]$.
facts: Continuous on $[a,b]$ $\Rightarrow$ bounded, attains max and min, and is uniformly continuous.

en.q: Choose the wrong statement
options: every non abelian group has abelian subgroup
Every element generates a cyclic subgroup of its own order
a subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic
en.explanation: Klein's four-group $\{e,a,b,c\}$ with $a^2=b^2=c^2=e$ and $ab=c$ is abelian; indeed any group with $x^2=e$ for all $x$ is abelian. The other three statements are true.
notes: True: $\{e\}$, or any $\langle g\rangle$, is abelian.
facts: Klein's group $V_4\cong\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$: abelian, not cyclic, every non-identity element of order 2.

en.q: What are maximal subgroups of Klein's group?
en.explanation: $V_4=\{e,a,b,c\}$ has proper subgroups $\{e\}$, $\{e,a\}$, $\{e,b\}$, $\{e,c\}$. Each subgroup of order 2 has index 2, so no subgroup lies strictly between it and $V_4$: all three are maximal. The official key (a) $\{e,c\}$ is wrong: $\{e,a\}$ and $\{e,b\}$ are maximal in exactly the same way (an automorphism of $V_4$ permutes $a,b,c$), so the maximal subgroups are all three, option (b).
notes: Correct: all three subgroups of order 2.
facts: A subgroup of prime index is maximal; $V_4$ has three maximal subgroups, all of order 2.

en.q: The symmetric property in a metric space is
en.explanation: Metric axioms: $d(x,y)\ge0$ with $d(x,y)=0\iff x=y$; symmetry $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$; triangle inequality $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: A metric is non-negative, zero only on the diagonal, symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality.

en.q: Integrate $\frac{1}{(z^3-1)^2}$, the counter clockwise around the circle $|z-1|=1$?
en.explanation:
The poles are the cube roots of unity, each double. Only $z=1$ lies inside, since $|\omega-1|=\sqrt3>1$. Write $f=\frac{g(z)}{(z-1)^2}$ with $g(z)=(z^2+z+1)^{-2}$.
$\operatorname{Res}_{z=1}f=g'(1)$, where $g'(z)=\frac{-2(2z+1)}{(z^2+z+1)^3}$, so the residue is $-\frac{6}{27}=-\frac29$.
Integral $=2\pi i\left(-\frac29\right)=-\frac{4\pi i}9$.
notes: $2\pi i$ times the residue was halved.
facts: At a double pole: $\operatorname{Res}_{z=a}\frac{g(z)}{(z-a)^2}=g'(a)$.

en.q: Number of onto homomorphisms from Klein's group to Symmetric group of order 4?
en.explanation: An onto homomorphism needs the image to be all of $S_4$, with $24$ elements. But the image of a group of order $4$ has order dividing $4$. So no onto homomorphism exists.
facts: $|f(G)|$ divides $|G|$, so an onto map $G\to H$ needs $|H|$ to divide $|G|$.

en.q: The external direct product of two groups is abelian if and only if?
en.explanation: In $G\times H$: $(a,b)(c,d)=(ac,bd)$ and $(c,d)(a,b)=(ca,db)$. These agree for all elements iff $ac=ca$ for all $a,c\in G$ and $bd=db$ for all $b,d\in H$, i.e. both $G$ and $H$ are abelian.
notes: Then the product is not abelian.
If the other factor is non-abelian, so is the product.
facts: $G\times H$ is abelian iff $G$ and $H$ are; cyclic iff both are cyclic with coprime orders.

en.q: Let $K$ be a group with $8$ elements. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $K$ and $H<K$. It is known that the size of $H$ is at least $3$. The size of $H$ is?
en.explanation: By Lagrange's theorem $|H|$ divides $8$: $1,2,4$ or $8$. $H$ is a proper subgroup, so $|H|\ne8$, and $|H|\ge3$ leaves $|H|=4$.
facts: Lagrange: the order of a subgroup divides the order of a finite group.

en.q: How many real roots are possible for the equation $x^5-x^4+x^3-1=0$?
en.explanation: A real polynomial of odd degree has at least one real root. Here $x=1$ is a root: $x^5-x^4+x^3-1=(x-1)(x^4+x^2+x+1)$, and $x^4+x^2+x+1=x^4+(x+\frac12)^2+\frac34>0$. So there is exactly one real root.
notes: Odd degree forces a real root.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: An odd-degree real polynomial has at least one real root; complex roots come in conjugate pairs.

en.q: What will be the minimum degree of polynomial with integer coefficients, having roots $2-\sqrt5$, $3$, $4$?
en.explanation: With integer (rational) coefficients, an irrational root $a-\sqrt b$ comes with its conjugate $a+\sqrt b$. So the roots include $2\pm\sqrt5$, $3$, $4$: minimum degree $4$, e.g. $(x^2-4x-1)(x-3)(x-4)$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: For rational coefficients, roots $a\pm\sqrt b$ come in pairs; for real coefficients, roots $p\pm iq$ come in pairs.

en.q: Which theorem connects the result $\langle T(x),y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$?
en.explanation: For a bounded operator $T$ on a Hilbert space and a fixed $y$, $x\mapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle$ is a bounded linear functional. By the Riesz representation theorem it equals $\langle x,z\rangle$ for a unique $z$; writing $z=T^*y$ defines the adjoint $T^*$.
notes: Hahn–Banach extends linear functionals; it does not represent them.
Picard's theorems are about ODE existence or entire functions.
facts: Riesz: every bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space is $x\mapsto\langle x,z\rangle$ for a unique $z$.

en.q: If $u=(1,0,1)$, $v=(0,1,1)$ find the cosine of angle between these two vectors using inner product?
en.explanation: $\cos\theta=\frac{\langle u,v\rangle}{\|u\|\|v\|}$, which is $\frac{0+0+1}{\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2}=\frac12$, so $\theta=60^\circ$.
facts: $\cos\theta=\frac{\langle u,v\rangle}{\|u\|\|v\|}$.

en.q: Find the residue of $\frac{2z+1}{(z+1)(z-1)}$ at $z=1$?
en.explanation: $z=1$ is a simple pole: $\operatorname{Res}_{z=1}=\lim_{z\to1}(z-1)f(z)=\frac{2(1)+1}{1+1}=\frac32$.
facts: Simple pole: $\operatorname{Res}_{z=a}\frac{p(z)}{q(z)}=\frac{p(a)}{q'(a)}$.

en.q: Find the residue of $\frac{z^3}{z^2-1}$ at $z=\infty$?
en.explanation: For large $|z|$: $\frac{z^3}{z^2-1}=z\left(1-\frac1{z^2}\right)^{-1}$, that is $z+\frac1z+\frac1{z^3}+\dots$. The residue at $\infty$ is minus the coefficient of $\frac1z$: $-1$. Check: the residues at $\pm1$ are $\frac12+\frac12=1$, and all residues add up to $0$.
facts: $\operatorname{Res}_{z=\infty}f=-(\text{coefficient of }1/z)$; the sum of all residues, including $\infty$, is $0$.

en.q: Choose the wrong statement
options: If $R$ is integral domain then $R[x]$ is also an integral domain
If $R$ is integral domain then units of $R$ and $R[x]$ are same
en.explanation: If $R$ is a commutative ring with unity (CRU), so is $R[x]$, with the constant $1$ as unity; so (c) is wrong. (a) and (b) hold because degrees add in a domain: $\deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g$. (d) holds since $1,x,x^2,\dots$ are distinct.
notes: True: leading coefficients multiply to a non-zero element.
True: a unit must have degree $0$.
facts: $R$ an integral domain $\Rightarrow$ $R[x]$ is an integral domain with the same units; $R[x]$ is never a field.

en.q: Evaluate the integral $\int_C\frac1z\,dz$ where $C$ is the circle $z=e^{ib}$ where $0<b<\pi$?
en.explanation: On $z=e^{ib}$, $dz=ie^{ib}\,db$, so $\int_C\frac{dz}z=\int_0^\pi i\,db=\pi i$. ($C$ is the upper half of the unit circle, from $1$ to $-1$; the full circle would give $2\pi i$.)
notes: $C$ is an open arc, not a closed curve: the integral is $i$ times the change in $\arg z$, here $\pi$.
facts: $\oint_{|z|=r}\frac{dz}z=2\pi i$; over an arc of angle $\alpha$ the integral is $i\alpha$.

en.q: Which of the following is not a polynomial ring?
en.explanation: $\mathbb Q[x]$, $\mathbb C[x]$ and $\mathbb R[x]$ are polynomial rings over fields. The set difference $\mathbb R[x]-\mathbb Z[x]$ does not contain $0$, and is not closed under addition ($\frac x2+\frac x2=x$), so it is not a ring at all.
facts: For a ring $R$, $R[x]$ is a ring; a set difference of rings is never a ring (it lacks $0$).
